title: Persecutions
hook: monasteries closed in Tang China and temples torn down in Japan when Buddhism was split from the state

segments.voice: Yesterday: the dhammaraja ideal, Ajatasattu's errand, Ashoka's remorse, the sangha held close by power. Your line: protected and used.

A bronze Buddha goes into a furnace and comes out as coins. That scene, or one like it, belongs to a stretch of Chinese history when an emperor of the Tang dynasty turned on the monasteries. A Japanese monk named Ennin happened to be traveling in China then, and he kept a diary: monks and nuns sent back to lay life, temples emptied, images taken away, foreign monks like himself ordered to leave. Yesterday the power that protected the sangha also used it. Today it turns against it.

Start with China. Under the Tang emperor Wuzong, the court ordered monasteries closed and their lands and metal taken, and monks and nuns were made to return to ordinary life. Accounts point to more than one reason: money, land, bronze, and court politics that favored other teachings. Ennin's diary is one of the eyewitness sources. Now Japan, much later. A new government set out to separate Buddhist and Shinto institutions, which had been woven together for a long time, and in some regions a movement rose under a harsh slogan, haibutsu kishaku: abolish the Buddha, destroy Shakyamuni. Temples were closed or torn down, images burned or sold, and some monks forced out of their robes. Neither story is told to cast anyone as a villain. Each is told because it happened. Then the second half, today's line: it endured. In China, practice went on, in small temples, in homes, in the chanting of the Buddha's name, and later rulers allowed monasteries again. In Japan, temples were rebuilt and communities regathered. The Buddha's last words, in the discourse on his final passing, already pointed at this. In Rhys Davids' translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Buildings are component things. So is bronze. So are estates. What came through the furnace was people, still practicing.

Bring to mind something in your life, or your family's, that came through a hard time: a recipe carried across a border, a prayer a grandparent kept saying when it wasn't safe, a friendship that survived a bad year. Notice that the building, the job, the house may be gone, and the thing itself is still here. Breathe with it, and let yourself honor it.
Persecutions. Times when rulers turned on monasteries, in Tang China and in Japan, and took the buildings, but not the practice.
Your line: it endured. The furnace took the bronze, not the people. Day one thousand thirty-three, done.

howItsDone: Buddhist communities in China and Japan remember these persecutions in their histories, and temples that were closed or destroyed have in places been rebuilt and are active today.

original.note: Japanese haibutsu kishaku: abolish the Buddha, destroy Shakyamuni; the name of the movement against temples.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism has always been safe and protected.
what it means: rulers have turned on the sangha too, closing monasteries and destroying temples, and the practice endured.
what a scholar hears: the Huichang persecution under Wuzong, recorded in Ennin's travel diary, and haibutsu kishaku after the Meiji separation of Shinto and Buddhism (shinbutsu bunri).
recall: a king who rules by dhamma

chat.says: If temples were torn down in China and Japan, how did Buddhism survive there?
options: Practice went on in homes, small temples and chanting, and later temples were rebuilt.
It didn't; it vanished from both lands and was brought back from India.
The emperors soon apologized and repaid every temple the very next year.
chat.meaning: Rulers took the buildings, bronze and land, but practice went on in homes, small temples and chanting, and later temples were allowed and rebuilt.

notes: Editor: cut the unsourced historians' claim that low-property forms of practice recovered fastest (claims rule: not in the cited texts); 'historians point to' changed to 'accounts point to'.

Claims rule: no years in the voice. The index hook gives 845 (Huichang persecution) and 'after 1868' (Meiji shinbutsu bunri); the hook field and voice avoid both. Confirm the general phrasing ('much later', 'when a new government came to power').

Ennin's diary: an eyewitness account of the Huichang persecution, including laicization of monks and nuns, confiscation, and the expulsion of foreign monks. Confirm the summary. The furnace image in the hook is framed as 'that scene, or one like it'; bronze images were melted for coin. Confirm.
Causes of the persecution (fiscal, land, metal, court favor for Daoism) are summarized as 'court politics that favored other teachings' to avoid making Daoists a foil. Confirm.
'Some historians note that the forms of practice that needed the least property tended to recover fastest' (commonly said of Chan and Pure Land after 845); attributed. Confirm or cut.
haibutsu kishaku glossed 'abolish the Buddha, destroy Shakyamuni'; kanji 廃仏毀釈 to confirm. Described as occurring 'in some regions'.
Rhys Davids' DN 16 VI.10 quoted; confirm exact wording and punctuation.
howItsDone 'in places been rebuilt' is general; confirm.
